The attackers set up automated monitoring systems on the compromised routers that watch for specific security and network management programs trying to run.

When defenders attempt to launch diagnostic tools or administrative utilities to investigate suspicious activity, the malware immediately detects these programs and kills them before they can complete their work.

The system works by checking each running process against a list and terminating anything that doesn't contain a special marker that only the attackers' own tools possess.

This creates a persistent defensive shield around the infection that actively blocks investigation attempts while allowing the botnet's command tools to operate freely.

The technique is called Event Triggered Execution because the malware responds automatically to the event of a new program starting, rather than requiring constant manual intervention from the attackers.

By embedding this monitoring capability directly into the compromised devices, the attackers ensure their control persists even if defenders become aware something is wrong.

The infected routers and network devices from the earlier compromise now serve a dual purpose as both attack infrastructure and self-protecting assets that resist cleanup efforts.

This makes remediation significantly harder because the standard tools security teams would normally use to examine and fix infected systems are prevented from running at all.

The business impact is that once these devices are compromised, they become extremely difficult to recover without complete reinstallation, and during that time they continue serving the attacker's botnet operations while blocking defensive responses.

To achieve this, they employed a technique called Event Triggered Execution. Essentially, this involves setting up the system to automatically execute certain actions when specific events occur. In this case, the attackers are monitoring the processes running on the compromised devices. They have configured the system to automatically terminate any network or administrative tools that don't contain a particular identifier. This clever move ensures that only their tools can operate, effectively blocking defenders from using common utilities to investigate or clean up the infection.

This could be anything from a user logging on to the system to a particular application being run. By modifying these event triggers to point to their malicious content, the attackers can ensure their code runs repeatedly, maintaining their access to the system.

Moreover, this technique can also be used to escalate privileges. By leveraging system mechanisms that execute code with higher permissions, such as those of a SYSTEM or service account, the attackers can gain greater control over the compromised system. This makes it even more challenging for defenders to detect and remove the malicious presence.

This persistence tactic is a testament to their strategic planning and understanding of system operations, allowing them to maintain control and continue their malicious activities undisturbed.

The attackers now shifted to making sure they could stay inside the network even if defenders discovered their initial entry points.

They did this through two main approaches that both focused on hiding their presence within legitimate network equipment.

First, they modified the actual software files running on the Ivanti Connect Secure appliances, which are the VPN devices that employees use to connect remotely to the company network. Think of this like secretly rewriting pages in an instruction manual that the device reads every time it starts up. By inserting malicious code directly into these legitimate system files, the attackers made their presence look like normal device operations. When security teams checked the device, everything appeared to be functioning as designed because the attackers had essentially become part of the device itself.

Second, they installed web shells on the compromised network devices. A web shell is a hidden remote access tool that sits on a web server and gives attackers a way to send commands and control the system through normal web traffic. It's like installing a secret back door that looks like regular website activity. The attackers deployed five different versions of these web shells across the compromised devices. This redundancy meant that even if security teams found and removed one or two of these hidden access points, the attackers still had other ways to get back in.

Both techniques gave the attackers what security professionals call persistence, which means the ability to maintain access over time regardless of system reboots, security scans, or initial cleanup efforts. By embedding themselves directly into the network infrastructure devices that handle remote access, the attackers positioned themselves in a place where they could monitor traffic, steal credentials, and move deeper into the organization whenever they wanted.
